name: Spacing effect
statement: Spreading study sessions apart in time produces better long-term retention than packing the same total study time into one sitting.
meaning: Two intervals define the claim. The interstudy interval is the gap between one encounter with the material and the next. The retention interval is the gap between the last encounter and the test. The spacing effect proper compares a gap of zero against any gap at all. The lag effect compares a short gap against a longer one, and it is the harder question, because longer is not always better. Expanding retrieval practice is a third claim again, about widening the gaps between successive tests, and it has its own record. Total study time is held constant, so the finding is about arrangement rather than effort. Cepeda and colleagues treat spacing and lag as one phenomenon with a single control variable, the interstudy interval, and their central result is that its best value depends on when the test falls.

origin.where: Über das Gedächtnis, translated as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology
origin.note: Chapter VIII, section 34. Ebbinghaus learned 12-syllable series on himself. Massing 68 repetitions on one day let him recite a series without error the next day after 7 further repetitions. Spreading 38 repetitions over the three preceding days bought the same saving, at about 6 repetitions. He drew the conclusion narrowly, calling it probable that a suitable distribution over a space of time beats massing, and writing that he had found it for only very limited conditions. The subject count was one.

evidence: Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted and Rohrer assembled 839 assessments of distributed practice from 317 experiments in 184 articles, restricted to verbal recall. On the spaced-against-massed comparison, 271 performance differences from 254 studies covered 14,811 participants. Spaced conditions recalled 47.3% against 36.7% massed, t(540) = 6.6, p < .001. Only 12 of those 271 comparisons showed no effect or a negative one. The review reports percentage points rather than a pooled standardised effect, because only 23 of the 271 comparisons carried the data to compute one. Two findings run against each other. For the spacing effect proper the authors write that they failed to find any evidence that the effect is modulated by retention interval. For absolute lag the optimal interstudy interval rose with retention interval: gaps under a minute maximised retention at test delays under a minute, while gaps of at least a month maximised it at test delays of six months or more. Cepeda and colleagues then ran the experiment the literature lacked. They combined gap and retention interval into 26 conditions on an internet panel, and 1,354 subjects completed all three sessions. Noncompletion rose at the longer delays. Subjects learned 32 obscure trivia facts to a criterion of one perfect recall. Review followed after gaps of 0 to 105 days, and the final test came 7, 35, 70 or 350 days after that review. Against a zero gap, the best gap raised final recall by 64%, d = 1.1, and final recognition by 26%, d = 1.5. The size of that gain varied by test delay: 10%, 59%, 111% and 77% for the four retention intervals in recall.

replication.headline: Spacing survives the move out of the laboratory: a 2025 meta-analysis of classroom studies pooled 31 effect sizes and found d = 0.54, 95% CI [0.31, 0.77].
replication.detail: Mawson and Kang screened over 3,000 articles for classroom studies using curriculum materials and timescales a school would recognise, and kept 22 reports carrying 31 effect sizes across more than 3,000 learners. The pooled estimate was d = 0.54, 95% CI [0.31, 0.77], z = 4.631, p < .001. Heterogeneity was heavy, Q(30) = 230.33, p < .001, with more than 92% of between-study variance attributed to systematic influence. Egger's test found significant funnel asymmetry, z = 2.719, p = .007, which the authors read as small-study bias rather than publication bias, since many of the studies they collected were non-significant. Their abstract reports larger effect sizes alongside longer retention intervals, higher education levels and fewer re-exposures. Those are descriptive groupings, not tested moderators. Retention interval could not be used as a moderator at all, because several included studies had unequal or unspecified ones, and the one moderator they did fit, learning domain, came out non-significant, Q(8) = 7.56, p = .478. Murray, Horner and Göbel put the same question to mathematics in 2025 and got a smaller answer: g = 0.282, 95% CI [0.188, 0.376], from 27 studies and 53 effect sizes. Splitting by design gave g = 0.427, 95% CI [0.179, 0.675], where a skill was taught in isolation, against g = 0.24, 95% CI [0.155, 0.324], where practice sat inside a course. Two small studies are widely cited as classroom evidence, and Mawson and Kang screened out both. Sobel, Cepeda and Kapler taught eight GRE words to fifth-graders in their own classroom, four massed a minute apart and four spaced by a week, so each child served in both conditions. They recruited 46 and analysed 39. Definition recall five weeks later was 20.8% spaced against 7.5% massed, t(38) = 3.0, p = .004, d = 0.48. Mawson and Kang excluded it because postgraduate exam vocabulary is not what those children were studying. Kapler, Weston and Wiseheart gave undergraduates a 45-minute meteorology lecture, sent an online review after one day or eight, and tested 35 days after the review. They recruited 175 and analysed 169. The eight-day group scored higher on factual questions, 0.54 against 0.47, F(1,166) = 5.89, p = .02, and on higher-level questions, 0.42 against 0.35, F(1,166) = 4.71, p = .03. Its own title calls the classroom simulated, and Mawson and Kang excluded it as a laboratory study.

study.cite: Mawson, R. D., & Kang, S. H. K. (2025). The distributed practice effect on classroom learning: A meta-analytic review of applied research. Behavioral Sciences, 15(6), 771.

replicated.weighting: pooled across 31 effect sizes from 22 classroom reports

limits: The effect shrinks as the task gets harder. Donovan and Radosevich pooled 63 studies and 112 effect sizes for an overall d = 0.46, 95% CI [0.42, 0.50], then found that the number did not survive its own moderators. Heterogeneity was significant, Q(111) = 1025.25, p < .01. Their four task clusters gave d = 0.97 for tasks low in complexity and mental demand and high in physical demand, 0.42 for mentally demanding tasks of average complexity, and 0.11 and 0.07 for the two high-complexity clusters. Rated overall complexity correlated negatively with effect size, r = -.25, p < .05. Methodological rigour did the same: their lowest rigour band returned d = 1.22 against 0.40 for both higher bands, scored on a nine-item checklist. Their spaced conditions are also mostly rest breaks inside a session. Of the 88 effect sizes that reported an intertrial interval, 26 fell under a minute, 31 between one and ten minutes, 10 between ten minutes and an hour, and 21 over a day. Within that range shorter intervals gave larger effects, 0.71 under a minute falling to 0.16 beyond a day. That is the opposite of the day-scale pattern. The 2006 review's scope is verbal recall, so it carries no claim about motor skill or problem solving. The 2008 experiment ran on a self-selected internet panel with noncompletion rising at longer delays, and its materials were single-word answers to trivia questions. Mathematics is the weak case. Mawson and Kang found mathematics effect sizes smaller and more often non-significant, and offer the demand of transferring learning to novel situations as a possible reason. Murray and colleagues put course-embedded mathematics at g = 0.24. A 2026 meta-analysis of nine randomised trials in health professions education reports Hedges' g = 0.69, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.88, for knowledge acquisition and g = 0.62, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.82, for retention, with a high overall risk of bias. Its full text is behind a paywall at Elsevier and those figures were read from the abstract at Europe PMC, so they stay out of the structured fields here. Searching for later or larger work on 17 August 2026 covered Crossref, Europe PMC and general web search for meta-analyses of spacing or distributed practice published since 2023, and turned up the Mawson, Murray and Sezgin papers above and nothing else.
misreadings: The advice usually attached to the effect is more precise than the evidence behind it. The most common version, that the gap should be a fixed proportion of the retention interval, is contradicted by the study people cite for it. In Cepeda and colleagues' 2008 data the interpolated optimal gaps for retention intervals of 7, 35, 70 and 350 days were about 3, 8, 12 and 27 days, which the paper gives as 43%, 23%, 17% and 8% of the delay. The proportion falls as the delay grows; only the absolute gap rises. Their own summary is that the optimally efficient gap is not an absolute quantity that can be recommended, and that a learner has to decide first how long the material must last. Expanding schedules are the second error. Karpicke and Roediger compared expanding and equal schedules of retrieval practice on GRE vocabulary and found expanding ahead at 10 minutes, 71% against 62%, d = 0.30, and behind at two days, 33% against 45%, d = 0.50. Delaying the first attempt, not widening the later ones, carried the benefit. Those schedules were built from retrieval attempts, which is a separate literature. The 2006 review reached the same place on study repetitions: 62.0% for expanding against 58.6% for fixed across 22 comparisons in 18 studies, t(42) = 0.5, p = .61. Its verdict was that expanding intervals in general either help or match fixed spacing, and that examples of both run in the literature. Software that schedules by expanding interval is built on that gap. A third error runs the complexity relationship backwards, assuming difficult material gains most from spacing, where Donovan and Radosevich found the largest effects on the simplest tasks. And the striking classroom percentages measure small numbers. Sobel's 177% advantage is 20.8% recalled against 7.5%.
